summary: Defines how OAuth 2.0 clients can register themselves dynamically with an authorization server. The client sends metadata about itself and gets back a client identifier to use later.

eli5.summary: Instead of calling ahead to get a badge, an app fills out a form and gets one on the spot.

questions: what is oauth dynamic client registration
what is a software statement in oauth
what is the client registration endpoint
subtitle: How an OAuth 2.0 client signs itself up with an authorization server and gets its client identifier on the fly.

tldr.problem: An OAuth 2.0 client needs a client identifier and other details registered at an authorization server before it can use it, and that registration was traditionally done by hand.
tldr.mechanism: The client or its developer sends a JSON document of client metadata in an HTTP POST to a client registration endpoint, optionally with an initial access token and a signed software statement, and the server replies with a client identifier and any secret.
tldr.outcome: Clients can register themselves or be registered programmatically with many servers. The server must still treat the metadata as self-asserted unless a trusted software statement vouches for it.

today: RFC 7591 is a Proposed Standard, and no RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It points to RFC 7592 as an example of a mechanism for managing registrations afterwards.

sections.title: Registering Clients Without Paperwork
sections.content:
To use an OAuth 2.0 authorization server (RFC 6749), a client needs information about the server and an OAuth 2.0 client identifier issued by it. RFC 7591 describes how a client can be dynamically registered to obtain that. Traditionally registration was done manually.

The mechanism can be used by a client to register itself, or by a client developer to register the client programmatically. As part of the request the client presents metadata such as its valid redirection URIs, either as plain self-asserted values or as a software statement, a signed or MACed set of metadata in which an issuer vouches for the data.

The document generalizes registration mechanisms from OpenID Connect Dynamic Client Registration 1.0 and the User Managed Access (UMA) profile of OAuth 2.0, compatibly with both, but for a wider range of OAuth 2.0 uses.
sections.eli5: Normally a person has to fill in forms by hand to register an app. This lets the app, or its maker, do it by computer.

sections.title: Client Metadata
sections.content:
Metadata is a set of values tied to a client identifier at the server. It is used as input in registration requests and as output in responses, represented as JSON. Using each field is OPTIONAL unless stated otherwise.

The fields include redirect_uris (servers supporting redirect-based flows MUST support it), token_endpoint_auth_method, grant_types, response_types, client_name, client_uri, logo_uri, scope, contacts, tos_uri, policy_uri, jwks_uri, jwks, software_id and software_version. If omitted, token_endpoint_auth_method defaults to client_secret_basic, grant_types to only authorization_code, and response_types to only code. The fields jwks_uri and jwks MUST NOT both appear in the same request or response.

The software_id identifies the client software and SHOULD stay the same across all instances and versions, unlike the server-issued client_id, which SHOULD vary between instances. A server SHOULD stop a client from registering an inconsistent combination, for example authorization_code without the code response type, by returning invalid_client_metadata.

Human-readable fields may carry several languages by adding a BCP 47 language tag to the member name, separated by a hash character (for example a Japanese name for client_name). The server MUST ignore metadata it does not understand and MAY replace requested values with defaults or reject them.
sections.eli5: The form has boxes for the app's name, its picture, where to send people back to, and how it will prove who it is. The desk ignores any box it does not recognize.

sections.title: Software Statements and Initial Access Tokens
sections.content:
A software statement is a JSON Web Token (RFC 7519) that asserts metadata about the client software as a bundle. When presented, it MUST be signed or MACed using JSON Web Signature (RFC 7515) and MUST contain an iss claim naming the party vouching for it. Signing with RS256 is RECOMMENDED, and including software_id is RECOMMENDED. If the same field appears both in the statement and as a plain JSON member, and the server trusts the statement, the statement's value MUST take precedence. Whether to trust a statement is outside the scope of the RFC.

An initial access token is an OAuth 2.0 access token that limits who may call the registration endpoint. How it is issued and validated is out of scope, and it is required when the server restricts who can register. It represents permission to use the endpoint, not information about a particular piece of software.

An authorization server MUST consider the full request, meaning the software statement, the initial access token and the JSON metadata, when deciding whether to honor it.
sections.eli5: A software statement is like a note signed by someone the desk trusts, saying this app is who it claims to be. An initial access token is a pass that lets you use the desk at all.

sections.title: The Registration Request
sections.content:
The client registration endpoint MUST accept HTTP POST messages whose body is application/json, and it MUST be protected by transport-layer security. The body is one JSON object with all requested metadata as top-level members. A software statement goes in the optional software_statement member as a string holding the entire signed JWT.

The endpoint MAY be an OAuth 2.0 protected resource that accepts an initial access token, for example as a Bearer Token (RFC 6750), to limit registration to previously authorized parties. To support open registration, it SHOULD also allow requests with no authorization, although these MAY be rate-limited against denial of service.

The server assigns a unique client identifier, optionally a client secret, and stores the supplied metadata. It MAY provision defaults for omitted items. If it supports software statements, values in the statement MUST win over plain JSON values, and it MAY ignore a statement if it does not support the feature.
sections.eli5: The app sends its filled-in form to one special address, in a standard format, over a protected line. It can include its pass and its signed note if it has them.

sections.title: Responses and Errors
sections.content:
On success the server answers HTTP/1.1 201 Created with a JSON body. It contains client_id (REQUIRED), and client_secret (OPTIONAL, issued to confidential clients). If a secret is issued, client_secret_expires_at is REQUIRED, giving the expiry time or 0 if it does not expire. The optional client_id_issued_at is also available. Times are in seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z. The server MUST return all registered metadata, including fields it chose itself, and it MAY have replaced requested values. The client should compare the response with what it asked for and decide whether the result is good enough.

If a software statement was used, it MUST be returned unmodified in software_statement, and the metadata used from it MUST also appear as top-level members.

On failure, the server returns HTTP 400 (unless otherwise specified) with a JSON object containing error (REQUIRED) and optionally error_description. The defined codes are invalid_redirect_uri, invalid_client_metadata, invalid_software_statement and unapproved_software_statement. Updating a registration later is the job of a management protocol such as RFC 7592, which this document only mentions as optional.
sections.eli5: If the form is fine, the desk hands back a badge number, and maybe a secret password, along with a copy of what it actually recorded. If something is wrong, it says what in a short error note.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Requests and responses carry clear-text credentials, so the server MUST require transport-layer security and MUST support TLS 1.2. Clients MUST check the server certificate. Servers MUST require registered redirection URIs for redirect-based grant types, and each URI MUST be a TLS-protected remote site, an HTTP site on the local machine, or a non-HTTP application-specific URL available only to the client app.

Unless carried in a software statement, all metadata MUST be treated as self-asserted. A rogue client might copy a legitimate client's name, logo, software_id or software_version. The server should look at the whole request, for instance warning if the logo's domain differs from the redirection URIs' domain, or refusing a known software_id that asks for different redirection URIs. If a duplicate registration is inferred, the server SHOULD treat it as suspect and reject it.

With open registration, the server must be very careful with URLs shown to users (logo_uri, tos_uri, client_uri, policy_uri). It SHOULD check that they have the same host and scheme as the redirection URIs and resolve to valid pages, and may scan their content or show an interstitial warning. A server SHOULD NOT issue the same client secret to multiple instances, because a leak would let impostors impersonate a confidential client.
sections.eli5: Anyone can write anything on the form, so the desk must not believe it blindly. It checks that the name, picture and links make sense together, and warns people about brand-new apps.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The protocol deals almost entirely with software, not people, so privacy concerns are few. The main exception is the contacts field, which names those responsible for the client. Its values are meant for display to end users and are visible to server administrators, so a developer may prefer a support or collective address over a personal one.

Client identifiers are often unique to one instance. For a native app installed on one person's device, an identifier could be used to track that person across OAuth transactions. Clients are forbidden from making up their own identifiers, since that would let an instance be tracked across colluding servers.
sections.eli5: The form is mostly about the app, not about you. The one exception is the contact address, which should be a shared support mailbox rather than a private one.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
RFC 7591 creates two registries. The "OAuth Dynamic Client Registration Metadata" registry holds client metadata names and descriptions, and the "OAuth Token Endpoint Authentication Methods" registry holds values for token_endpoint_auth_method. The initial authentication method values are none, client_secret_post and client_secret_basic.

Both use Specification Required after a two-week review on the oauth-ext-review@ietf.org mailing list, on the advice of Designated Experts. The initial metadata registry covers the fields in this document, including the response fields client_id, client_secret, client_id_issued_at and client_secret_expires_at.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of every box that can appear on the form, so new boxes get added in an orderly way.
